title: New York Seizes a Dozen Celebrity Deepfake Websites
gist: The Manhattan District Attorney's Office seized 12 domains used to share and sell nonconsensual celebrity deepfake videos depicting roughly 1,200 people, overwhelmingly women — likely the largest such takedown to date. Researchers call it proof that state-level enforcement works even amid fragmented regulation, while warning that creation tools, hosting infrastructure, and payment and affiliate systems remain untouched.

themes.theme: The seizure and its legal mechanics

insights.claim: Prosecutors in Manhattan announced the seizure of 12 domains used for unlawfully sharing, publishing, and selling celebrity deepfake videos, in what is described as likely the largest takedown of explicit deepfake websites to date.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: A local prosecutor, not a federal agency or platform, executed the largest enforcement action yet against synthetic sexual abuse material.
insights.quote: officials in New York have seized more than a dozen of the harmful sites

insights.claim: Around 1,200 people, overwhelmingly women, were depicted in nonconsensual sexual images and videos on the seized websites, including social media influencers, actors, activists, athletes, musicians, and politicians.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: The victim count quantifies the industrialized scale of celebrity deepfake abuse concentrated on just a dozen domains.
insights.quote: Around 1,200 people—overwhelmingly women—were depicted in nonconsensual sexual images and videos on the websites

insights.claim: The seizures were carried out under New York's criminal procedure laws via a seizure warrant issued by a New York State Supreme Court, with homepages replaced by 'THIS DOMAIN HAS BEEN SEIZED' takedown notices.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Domain seizure warrants are emerging as the fastest practical lever against offshore abusive content, bypassing platform moderation entirely.

insights.claim: The US Take It Down Act increasingly allows such images to be removed, with part of the law empowering law enforcement officials to take down and seize websites.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Federal statute now supplies the seizure authority that made this state-level action possible, a template other DAs can copy.

insights.claim: Investigations into who operates the websites and who uploaded the damaging videos remain ongoing, and the district attorney publicly urged potential victims to contact his office's cybercrime bureau.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Domain seizure is the first step, not the end state; operator identification determines whether the deterrent is real.
insights.quote: These horrific violations of privacy follow victims into their careers and personal lives and take an immense toll on emotional and mental well-being

insights.claim: Since deepfake technology first emerged at the end of 2017, a dark industry of websites, apps, and bots has appeared designed to undress photos of women or create graphic sexual videos, with outputs now increasingly realistic and generable in seconds.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Falling generation cost and rising realism mean enforcement must scale faster than model capability, not just faster than site count.
insights.quote: The images and videos are increasingly realistic and can be generated in seconds.

insights.claim: Deepfake abuse is more widely used against non-famous women and girls, often shared in private social media groups, than against celebrities — but celebrity cases drive the public conversation because famous victims can speak out.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Enforcement concentrated on public websites misses the private-group distribution channel where most harm occurs.
insights.quote: While deepfake technology is widely used against non-famous women and girls—often being shared in private social media groups—celebrities have spoken out

insights.claim: The seized sites were likely viewed millions of times, used names including phrases such as 'sex celebrity' or promises of 'real deepfakes,' and archived versions show individual videos watched tens of thousands of times, with one site claiming to have been online since 2018.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Eight years of uninterrupted operation shows how long an openly named abusive business can run before any enforcement arrives.
insights.quote: one of the websites claiming to have been online since 2018

insights.claim: Most videos were actual pornographic movies manipulated to show targets' faces instead of the original actors, and many appeared to be reposts of content originally shared on MrDeepFakes, a notorious platform taken offline after reporters unmasked its creators.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Content survives platform death through mirroring, so takedowns displace rather than delete the underlying library.
insights.quote: Most videos took the shape of actual pornographic movies, manipulated to instead show targets’ faces instead of the original actors

insights.claim: On at least two of the seized websites, elected officials were given dedicated profiles containing their name and position alongside a grid of manipulated videos using their likeness.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Structured, indexed targeting of officeholders turns deepfake porn into a political harassment and blackmail infrastructure.
insights.quote: On at least two of the seized websites, elected officials were given profiles containing their name and position, along with a grid of manipulated videos hosting their likeness

insights.claim: Research found 56 European politicians had been mentioned or appeared on the websites, along with 16 US politicians and two based in the UK.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Cross-border targeting of politicians makes this a national-security-adjacent problem, not just a content moderation one.

themes.theme: What enforcement proves and what it misses

insights.claim: A researcher who studies the deepfake creation ecosystem says the seized sites do not appear accessible even via VPNs from other locations, showing that meaningful coordinated enforcement is achievable even where regulation remains fragmented across jurisdictions.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Domain-level seizure defeats the standard VPN workaround, which is why it is more effective than geoblocking or platform bans.
insights.quote: This shows that meaningful, coordinated enforcement is achievable even where regulation itself remains fragmented across jurisdictions.

insights.claim: Effective intervention requires targeting the ecosystem at multiple points — the creation tools, their discovery and promotion, the hosting and technical infrastructure that keeps sites online, and the payment and affiliate systems that let operators monetize them.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Payment processors, hosts, and app stores are the chokepoints that will face pressure next if takedowns alone prove insufficient.
insights.quote: including the tools used for the creation of synthetic NCII, the discovery and promotion of these, the hosting and technical infrastructure that keeps them online, and the payment and affiliate systems
